The adjective agrees

In English, an adjective never changes. In Italian, it agrees in gender and number with the noun. There are two families.

masc. sing.fem. sing.masc. pl.fem. pl.
in -otranquillotranquillatranquillitranquille
in -egrandegrandegrandigrandi

The -o family: four forms, like the nouns libro / libri and casa / case.

The -e family: only two forms, -e in the singular and -i in the plural, for masculine and feminine alike. The adjective doesn't change for the feminine.

un quartiere tranquillo, una strada tranquillaa quiet neighborhood, a quiet street
i vicini gentili, le stanze grandithe kind neighbors, the big rooms

The trap: never an -s in the plural: le stanze grandi, not \"grandes\". And the noun and the adjective don't always have the same ending: il quartiere tranquillo, la stanza grande.

A masculine noun and a feminine noun together: the adjective goes in the masculine plural.

La cucina e il bagno sono nuovi.The kitchen and the bathroom are new. (In Italian, bagno is masculine.)
", "

Before or after the noun?

In Italian, the adjective usually goes after the noun — the opposite of English.

un appartamento luminoso, una strada rumorosaa bright apartment, a noisy street

Always after: colors (un balcone verde) and nationalities (un vicino francese). Long adjectives also almost always go after.

A few short, very common adjectives can also go before, as in English: buono, grande, piccolo, nuovo, vecchio. Both orders are correct: una casa piccola or una piccola casa. Bello changes form before a noun: for now, use it after essere (la casa è bella).

Buono before the noun

After the noun, buono is regular. Before a masculine singular noun, it loses its -o, exactly the way uno becomes un.

After the nounBefore the noun
un vino buonoun buon vino
un ristorante buonoun buon ristorante
una pizza buonauna buona pizza

If you're not sure, put the adjective after the noun: it's almost always correct.

", "

Molto: \"very\" or \"a lot of\"?

English uses different words here (very, a lot, many, much). Molto covers them all, but it behaves in two different ways.

UseMeaningAgreementExample
molto + adjectiveveryinvariableLe stanze sono molto grandi.
verb + moltoa lotinvariablePaolo lavora molto.
molto + nouna lot of, many, muchagrees with the nounmolto traffico, molta luce, molti negozi, molte finestre

Before a noun, no \"of\": molti negozi = a lot of stores. Don't say \"molto di negozi\".

La casa è molto bella e ha molte finestre.The house is very beautiful and it has a lot of windows.

The trick: if you'd translate it as \"very\" or as \"a lot\" on its own, molto doesn't change. If you'd translate it as \"a lot of\", \"many\" or \"much\", it agrees with the noun that follows.

title: Describing with adjectives
topic: adjective agreement; position; molto, variable or invariable
why: After present-tense verbs and the daily routine, the learner needs to be able to describe where they live. A slow lesson on a single point (the adjective: agreement, position, molto), with no new tense, reusing the regular present, negation, questions and reflexive verbs.
